title: Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? 0.2 Seconds Changes It 🤔
description:
Why can't you tickle yourself? Your cerebellum predicts the touch from your own movement and turns the feeling down, but in a robot experiment, adding a delay of just 0.2 seconds made self-tickling feel more ticklish.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-cant-a-person-tickle/
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/2870
https://www.sciencealert.com/the-scientific-reason-you-can-t-tickle-yourself

Animated in the Napkin Sketch style.
pinned_comment: Have you EVER managed to tickle yourself? Tell me how 👇
script: Your brain cancels your own tickles before you feel them. But how? Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the order to the cerebellum, at the back of your head. It predicts what the touch will feel like, then turns the feeling down. No surprise, no tickle. When someone else tickles you, there's no prediction. Your brain can't guess where or when, so it hits full blast. Scientists tested this with a robot. People moved a handle, and a robot brushed their palm. Moving it themselves? Barely ticklish. Then the robot added a delay of just two tenths of a second. Suddenly, it felt more ticklish. The prediction was off, so the brain couldn't cancel it. So your own brain blocks the tickle. Can you find a way to outsmart it?
key_facts: Every movement sends a copy of the motor command to the cerebellum, which predicts the sensory result and dampens it (Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith).
Touch from someone else can't be predicted, so it isn't dampened.
In a robot-arm experiment, delaying the self-produced touch by 0.2 seconds made it feel more ticklish.
